purpose: Prasugrel is used to prevent dangerous blood clots from forming in people who have had a heart attack or severe chest pain and have had a procedure called a stent placed in their arteries. It helps keep your blood flowing smoothly and reduces your risk of having another heart attack or stroke. It is usually used together with aspirin.
how_it_works: Your blood contains tiny cells called platelets that normally clump together to form clots and stop bleeding. In people with heart disease, these platelets can clump together inside arteries and cause a dangerous blockage. Prasugrel blocks a signal on platelets that tells them to clump, so your blood is less likely to form harmful clots.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is bleeding, which can show up as easy bruising, bleeding that takes longer than usual to stop, nosebleeds, or blood in your urine or stool. You may also notice headache, dizziness, or feeling short of breath. Some people develop a rash or have high blood pressure.
warnings: This medication can cause serious or life-threatening bleeding, so tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual bleeding anywhere on your body. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, especially if you have a stent, because stopping suddenly can increase your risk of a heart attack. This drug is generally not recommended for people 75 years or older or those who weigh less than 132 pounds (60 kg) due to a higher bleeding risk. Also tell your doctor if you have ever had a stroke or mini-stroke (TIA), as prasugrel is not safe for those patients.
typical_dosing: Most adults start with a one-time loading dose of 60 mg, then take 10 mg once a day with or without food. If you are under 60 kg (about 132 lbs), your doctor may lower your daily dose to 5 mg. Try to take it at the same time each day, and always take it exactly as your doctor prescribed.
